extracted.intended_audience: employers, labor representatives, occupational safety and health professionals, and stakeholders/commenters on the OSHA NPRM
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of the proposed OSHA Heat Injury and Illness Prevention standard requirements (NPRM) that employers must follow, including operational, training, compensation, and procedural provisions. Useful for employers implementing the HIIPP, compliance reviewers, and commenters on the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementation at no cost to employees (paragraph (j))
rubrics_metrics.description: The implementation of all requirements of this standard must be at no cost to the employee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA considers costs to include not only direct monetary expenses to the employee, but also the time and other expenses necessary to perform required tasks. This requirement applies to all provisions of the proposed standard, including employee time spent to implement or comply with those provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee input and involvement in HIIPP and monitoring plans (proposed (c)(6),(c)(7), (d)(3)(iv))
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must seek the input and involvement of non-managerial employees and their representatives, if any, in the development and implementation of the heat injury and illness prevention plan (HIIPP) and during any reviews or updates of the HIIPP; and when evaluating work sites to identify areas with reasonable expectation of exposures at/above the initial heat trigger and developing/updating monitoring plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employer must cover expenses of non-managerial employees for participation (e.g., travel costs) and must pay employees their normal rate of pay for time necessary to engage in development, implementation, reviews and updates of the HIIPP and monitoring plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of potable drinking water (proposed (e)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must provide access to potable water for drinking placed in locations readily accessible to the employee, suitably cool, and of sufficient quantity to provide access to 1 quart of drinking water per employee per hour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To ensure this is provided at no cost to employees, the employer must pay for the water, its container, and means to utilize the water (cups, bottles, etc.), and must pay employees their normal rate of pay for time necessary to consume water and any time necessary to travel to/from the water location. Example: if water is only available in a break room due to safety/toxic materials in the work area, the employer must pay walking/travel time plus consumption time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acclimatization protocol for new and returning employees (proposed (e)(7))
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must implement an acclimatization protocol for new and returning employees when they would be exposed to heat at or above the initial heat trigger, except when the employee consistently worked under the same or similar conditions within the prior 14 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For new employees (e)(7)(i) employer may choose either: (A) an acclimatization plan that at minimum includes measures in proposed paragraph (f) (rest breaks, observation for signs/symptoms, hazard alert, warning signs); or (B) gradual acclimatization restricting exposure to no more than 20% of a normal shift on day 1, 40% day 2, 60% day 3, and 80% day 4. For returning employees (e)(7)(ii) employer may choose either: (A) plan incorporating (f) during first week back when heat index at/above initial trigger; or (B) gradual acclimatization restricting exposure to 50% day 1, 60% day 2, and 80% day 3. Employers often may provide other work (e.g., indoor AC work) during restricted exposure so employees can work full shifts while meeting exposure limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation for restricted-acclimatization hours (part of (e)(7))
rubrics_metrics.description: If an employer restricts an employee's exposure as part of a gradual acclimatization plan (i.e., the employee works fewer heat-exposure hours than a normal shift), the employer must compensate the employee for the hours they would typically be expected to work (the employee's normal full shift) after acclimatization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a new employee expected to work an 8-hour shift but restricted to 4 hours of heat exposure on first day must be paid normal rate for the full 8-hour shift even if they worked only 4 hours of heat-exposed duties. Employers may provide alternate indoor or non-heat tasks so employees can work full shifts while restricted from heat exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paid rest breaks at or above initial/high heat triggers (proposed (e)(8) and (f)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Rest breaks required by the standard must be paid; employees must receive their normal rate of pay during rest breaks required by paragraphs (e)(8) and (f)(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For hourly employees, this means receiving the same hourly rate during rest breaks as while working. OSHA emphasizes paying employees during breaks so they are not financially penalized or discouraged from taking protections. (Note: elsewhere the proposal references a requirement of 15-minute rest breaks every two hours in high heat conditions as an example of a control in paragraph (f)(2)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Piece-rate employee rest-break compensation calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: For piece-rate employees, the proposed standard defines “normal rate of pay” for heat-related rest breaks by dividing total weekly pay by total hours worked during the week (excluding heat-related rest breaks) and multiplying that rate by the total heat-related rest break time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA provides the California approach (Cal. Lab. Code section 226.2) and an illustrative formula: e.g., if weekly pay=$600 and hours worked excluding heat breaks=37.5, normal rate for breaks = $600 ÷ 37.5 = $16/hour; total heat-break pay = $16 × total heat-break hours. Time for rest breaks under (e)(8) would be added to heat-related rest-break time per week. OSHA requests comment on alternative calculation approaches and whether to make the calculation explicit in paragraph (j).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relief from duty and paid recovery for symptomatic employees (proposed (g)(2)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: An employee experiencing signs and symptoms of heat-related illness must be relieved from duty, and the employer must pay the employee their normal pay while they are relieved from duty until the signs and symptoms subside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision requires immediate removal from work for symptomatic employees and continuation of normal pay during that time to remove financial disincentives to report symptoms or seek care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training on heat hazards provided at no cost and paid time (proposed (h))
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must provide training on heat hazards and associated protective measures at no cost to the employee, and must pay employees for time spent in training, including any time needed to travel to and from training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All training provided to meet the standard's requirements must be employer-provided at no employee cost; employer must pay for travel time to training as well as the training time itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective and compliance dates (paragraph (k))
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed standard would take effect 60 days after publication of the final standard in the Federal Register. Employers would be required to comply with all requirements 90 days after the effective date (150 days after publication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA states the 60-day effective period is to allow employers to familiarize themselves with the standard and 90 days (from effective date) is intended to allow adequate time to develop HIIPP, identify hazards, implement measures, and provide training. OSHA solicits comment on adequacy of these dates, alternative timeframes, and phased-in approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severability provision (paragraph (l))
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed standard contains an explicit severability clause: if any section, provision, or application is held invalid, stayed, or enjoined, the remaining sections and provisions should remain effective and operative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA expresses intent that each individual section remains workable independently and that courts should presume OSHA would have issued the remainder of the standard without the invalidated provision(s). Example: if a court invalidates the requirement for 15-minute rest breaks every two hours, remaining controls should still provide protections and the rest of the standard should stand.
